questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance $100\ \Omega$ gives full scale deflection for a current of $1$ mA. It is converted into an ammeter of range $0 - 10$ A. The shunt required is :
questions.solution:
Given $G = 100\ \Omega$, $I_g = 1\text{ mA} = 10^{-3}\text{ A}$, and $I = 10\text{ A}$.

The shunt resistance $S$ required to convert a galvanometer into an ammeter is given by:

$S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g}$

Substituting the values:

$S = \dfrac{10^{-3} \times 100}{10 - 10^{-3}}$

Since $10 \gg 10^{-3}$, we can approximate $10 - 10^{-3} \approx 10$.

$S \approx \dfrac{0.1}{10} = 0.01\ \Omega$

Answer: $0.01\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A room heater is rated $400$ W, $220$ V. If the supply voltage drops to $200$ V, what will be the power consumed (approximately) ?
questions.solution:
The resistance of the room heater is given by $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$

Substituting the rated values, $R = \dfrac{220^2}{400} = \dfrac{48400}{400} = 121 \Omega$

When the supply voltage drops to $V' = 200$ V, the power consumed is $P' = \dfrac{V'^2}{R}$

$P' = \dfrac{200^2}{121} = \dfrac{40000}{121} \approx 330.57$ W

Therefore, the power consumed is approximately $331$ W.

Answer: $331$ W

questions.q: A resistor is connected to a battery of $12$ V emf and internal resistance $2\ \Omega$. If the current in the circuit is $0.6$ A, the terminal voltage of the battery is :
questions.solution:
The terminal voltage $V$ of a battery discharging in a circuit is given by the relation:

$V = E - Ir$

Substituting the given values $E = 12$ V, $r = 2\ \Omega$, and $I = 0.6$ A:

$V = 12 - (0.6 \times 2)$

$V = 12 - 1.2$

$V = 10.8$ V

Answer: $10.8$ V

questions.q: Consider two circuits, (A) and (B), each having two resistors. One of them has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, $+\alpha$, while the other one has a negative temperature of coefficient, $-\alpha$, as shown in the figure. The current through these circuits are denoted by $I_A$ and $I_B$. At initial temperature, the resistance of the two resistors is $R_0$. As the temperature is increased, the correct option that describes the variation of current in these circuits is :
questions.solution:
For circuit (A), the two resistors are connected in series.
The equivalent resistance is given by:
$R_A = R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T) + R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T) = 2R_0$
The current in circuit (A) is $I_A = \dfrac{V}{R_A} = \dfrac{V}{2R_0}$.
Since $R_A$ is independent of the temperature change $\Delta T$, the current $I_A$ remains constant.

For circuit (B), the two resistors are connected in parallel.
The equivalent resistance is given by:
$R_B = \dfrac{R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T) \cdot R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)}{R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T) + R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)}$
$R_B = \dfrac{R_0^2(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)}{2R_0} = \dfrac{R_0}{2}(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)$
As the temperature increases, $\Delta T$ increases, which means the term $(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)$ decreases.
Therefore, the equivalent resistance $R_B$ decreases.
The current in circuit (B) is $I_B = \dfrac{V}{R_B}$.
Since $R_B$ decreases with an increase in temperature, the current $I_B$ increases.

Thus, $I_A$ remains constant while $I_B$ increases.

Answer: $I_A$ remains constant while $I_B$ increases

questions.q: A uniform wire of diameter $d$ carries a current of 100 mA when the mean drift velocity of electrons in the wire is $v$. For a wire of diameter $\frac{d}{2}$ of the same material to carry a current of 200 mA , the mean drift velocity of electrons in the wire is
questions.solution:
current $i=n A v_d \mathrm{e}$
( $v_d=$ mean drift velocity $)$
$=n\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right) v_d e$
$\therefore i \propto D^2 v_d$
$\frac{100}{200}=\frac{(d)^2}{\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2} \times \frac{v}{v^{\prime}}$
$\Rightarrow v^{\prime}=2 \times 2^2 v=8 v$

questions.q: In an electrical circuit, the voltage is measured as $V=(200 \pm 4)$ volt and the current is measured as $I=(20 \pm 0.2) \mathrm{A}$. The value of the resistance is:
questions.solution:
$R=\frac{V}{l}=\frac{200}{20}=10 \Omega$
$\frac{\Delta R}{R}=\frac{\Delta V}{V}+\frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{4}{200}+\frac{0.2}{20}=\frac{4+2}{200}=\frac{6}{200}$
$\Rightarrow \Delta R=\frac{6}{200} \times R=\frac{6}{20}=\frac{3}{10}=0.3 \Omega$
$\therefore$ Resistance $=R \pm \Delta R=(10 \pm 0.3) \Omega$

questions.q: A wire of length ' 1 and resistance $100 \Omega$ is divided into 10 equal parts. The first 5 parts are connected in series while the next 5 parts are connected in parallel. The two combinations are again connected in series. The resistance of this final combination is:
questions.solution:
Divided into 10 parts
$\begin{aligned}
R & =\frac{\rho l}{A} \\
R^{\prime} & =\frac{\rho l}{10 A}=\frac{R}{10} \\
R_S & =5 \times \frac{R}{10} \quad \text{ [series] } \\
R_S & =50 \\
R_P & =\frac{R}{50} \quad \text{ [parallel] } \\
R_{\text{eq }} & =R_S+R_P \\
& =52 \Omega
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $10$ resistors, each of resistance $R$ are connected in series to a battery of emf $E$ and negligible internal resistance. Then those are connected in parallel to the same battery, the current is increased $n$ times. The value of $n$ is:
questions.solution:
When the resistors are connected in series with the battery, the equivalent resistance $\left({R}_{s}\right)$ can be written as

$\begin{cases}{R}_{s} & = & R + R + . . . . 10times \\ & = & 10R . . . \left(1\right)\end{cases}$

Hence, the current $\left({i}_{s}\right)$ is given by

$\begin{cases}{i}_{s} & = & \dfrac{E}{{R}_{s}} \\ & = & \dfrac{E}{10R} . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

When the resistors are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance $\left({R}_{p}\right)$ is given by

$\begin{cases}{R}_{p} & = & \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{R} + \dfrac{1}{R} + . . . . 10times} \\ & = & \dfrac{R}{10} . . . \left(3\right)\end{cases}$

Hence, the current $\left({i}_{p}\right)$ is given by

$\begin{cases}{i}_{p} & = & \dfrac{E}{{R}_{p}} \\ & = & \dfrac{E}{\dfrac{R}{10}} \\ & = & \dfrac{10E}{R} . . . \left(4\right)\end{cases}$

Divide equation (4) by equation (2) to obtain the required value of the multiplier $n$.

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{{i}_{p}}{{i}_{s}} & = & \dfrac{\dfrac{10E}{R}}{\dfrac{E}{10R}} \\ & = & 100\end{cases}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform metallic wire having resistance $4\ \Omega$ is bent to form a square loop (ABCD) (see figure). A resistance of $2\ \Omega$ is connected between points B and D and a battery of $2$ V is connected across points A and C as shown in the figure. Now the value of current ($I$) is :
questions.solution:
The total resistance of the uniform wire is $4\ \Omega$. Since it is bent to form a square loop ABCD, the resistance of each of its four sides is equal.

Resistance of each side $= \dfrac{4}{4} = 1\ \Omega$.
Thus, $R_{AB} = R_{BC} = R_{CD} = R_{DA} = 1\ \Omega$.

The given circuit can be redrawn as a Wheatstone bridge where the arms are AB, BC, AD, and DC, and the central arm is BD. The battery is connected across the opposite corners A and C.

Let's check the balance condition of the Wheatstone bridge:
$\dfrac{R_{AB}}{R_{AD}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$
$\dfrac{R_{BC}}{R_{DC}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = 1$

Since $\dfrac{R_{AB}}{R_{AD}} = \dfrac{R_{BC}}{R_{DC}}$, the Wheatstone bridge is balanced. This means the potential at point B is equal to the potential at point D ($V_B = V_D$).

Therefore, no current will flow through the $2\ \Omega$ resistor connected between B and D, and it can be removed from the circuit for calculation.

Now, the circuit simplifies to two parallel branches across the battery:
1. Upper branch (A $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ C) with resistance $R_1 = R_{AB} + R_{BC} = 1 + 1 = 2\ \Omega$.
2. Lower branch (A $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ C) with resistance $R_2 = R_{AD} + R_{DC} = 1 + 1 = 2\ \Omega$.

The equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ of the circuit is the parallel combination of $R_1$ and $R_2$:
$\dfrac{1}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\ \Omega^{-1}$
$\Rightarrow R_{eq} = 1\ \Omega$

The total current $I$ drawn from the battery is given by Ohm's law:
$I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{2\text{ V}}{1\ \Omega} = 2\text{ A}$.

Answer: $2$ A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As the temperature increases, the electrical resistance
options: decreases for both conductors and semiconductors
increases for conductors but decreases for semiconductors
decreases for conductors but increases for semiconductors
increases for both conductors and semiconductors
questions.solution:
For conductors, on increasing temperature, thermal agitation of free electrons increases. Hence, resistance increases.

For Semiconductors, number of holes or charge carriers increases with increase in temperature.

Hence, resistance increases for conductors but decreases for semiconductors.

$⇒$ Answer is (b)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a metre bridge experiment (see figure), the positions of the cell, $E$, and galvanometer, $G$, are interchanged. We shall observe in the galvanometer :
options: There will be no deflection irrespective of the position of the jockey
Both right-sided and left-sided deflection and at balance point, no deflection
questions.solution:
Let the nodes of the circuit be identified as follows:
Node A: Left L-shaped metallic strip.
Node B: Right L-shaped metallic strip.
Node C: Central metallic strip.
Node D: The point on the wire where the jockey touches.

The resistances in the four arms of the circuit are:
1. Resistance between A and C is $R_1$.
2. Resistance between B and C is $R_2$.
3. Resistance between A and D is $R_{AD}$ (left part of the metre bridge wire).
4. Resistance between B and D is $R_{DB}$ (right part of the metre bridge wire).

In the given figure, the cell $E$ is connected between nodes C and D, and the galvanometer $G$ is connected between nodes A and B. This arrangement forms a Wheatstone bridge.

Let the potential at node D be $0$ and the potential at node C be $V$.
The current from the cell divides at node C into two parallel branches: C $\rightarrow$ A $\rightarrow$ D and C $\rightarrow$ B $\rightarrow$ D.
The potential at node A is given by the voltage divider rule:
$V_A = V \left( \dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_1 + R_{AD}} \right)$

Similarly, the potential at node B is:
$V_B = V \left( \dfrac{R_{DB}}{R_2 + R_{DB}} \right)$

The galvanometer shows no deflection when the potential difference across it is zero, i.e., $V_A = V_B$.
$\dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_1 + R_{AD}} = \dfrac{R_{DB}}{R_2 + R_{DB}}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R_1 + R_{AD}}{R_{AD}} = \dfrac{R_2 + R_{DB}}{R_{DB}}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R_1}{R_{AD}} + 1 = \dfrac{R_2}{R_{DB}} + 1$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{R_1}{R_{AD}} = \dfrac{R_2}{R_{DB}}$

This is the standard balance condition for a Wheatstone bridge. Thus, interchanging the cell and the galvanometer does not affect the balance condition. A null point will still be obtained on the wire.

If the jockey is moved to the left of the balance point, $R_{AD}$ decreases and $R_{DB}$ increases, making $V_A < V_B$. Current will flow from B to A through the galvanometer, causing a deflection in one direction.
If the jockey is moved to the right of the balance point, $R_{AD}$ increases and $R_{DB}$ decreases, making $V_A > V_B$. Current will flow from A to B, causing a deflection in the opposite direction.

Therefore, the galvanometer will show both right-sided and left-sided deflections depending on the jockey's position, and no deflection at the balance point.

Answer: Both right-sided and left-sided deflection and at balance point, no deflection

questions.q: A Wheatstone bridge is used to determine the value of unknown resistance $X$ by adjusting the variable resistance $Y$ as shown in the figure. For the most precise measurement of $X$, the resistances $P$ and $Q$
options: should be approximately equal and are small
should be very large and unequal
do not play any significant role
questions.solution:
For precise measurement of $X$, value of $X$ should be close to $Y$. Therefore, resistances $P$ and $Q$ should be equal.
If $P$ and $Q$ are large the current in the galvanometer will be small, and it will be difficult to find the null point. Therefore, $P$ and $Q$ should be small.

questions.q: A copper wire of length $10m$ and radius $\left(\dfrac{{10}^{- 2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)m$ has electrical resistance of $10Ω$. The current density in the wire for an electric field strength of $10V{m}^{- 1}$ is:
questions.solution:
Length $= 10m$

Radius $= \left(\dfrac{{10}^{- 2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)m$

Electrical resistance $= 10Ω$

Electric field strength $= 10V{m}^{- 1}$

Current density, $J = \dfrac{I}{A} = \dfrac{V}{RA} = \dfrac{EL}{RA}$

$⇒ J = \dfrac{10 \times 10}{10 \times \pi{\left(\dfrac{{10}^{- 2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)}^{2}} = {10}^{5}A{m}^{- 2}$

questions.q: The effective resistance of a parallel connection that consists of four wires of equal length, equal area of cross-section and same material is $0 . 25Ω$. What will be the effective resistance if they are connected in series?
questions.solution:
Let the resistance of each wire be $R$

Effective resistance in parallel combination,

${R}_{P} = \dfrac{R}{4}$

$⇒ R = 4{R}_{P}$

$⇒ R = 4 \times 0 . 25 = 1Ω$

Effective resistance is series combination,

${R}_{S} = 4R$

$⇒ {R}_{s} = 4 \times 1 = 4Ω$

For an ideal voltmeter, resistance is infinite $\left({R}_{V} = \infty\right)$, so it will not draw any amount of current from the circuit and for ideal ammeter resistance is zero.

$∴$ Ammeter and voltmeter readings for the second circuit is ${V}_{2} = 10V, {i}_{2} = 1A$

$∴$ For both the circuit is
${V}_{1} = {V}_{2} = 10V, {i}_{1} = {i}_{2} = 1A$

questions.q: A set of $n$ equal resistances, of value $R$ each, are connected in series to a battery of emf $E$ and internal resistances $R$. The current drawn is $I$. Now, the $n$ resistance are connected in parallel to the same battery. Then the current drawn from battery becomes $10I$. The value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
In the first case, it is given that 'n' resistances are arranged in series, each having a resistance R.

In that case, the nett reistance of the external circuit is 'nR'. The internal resistance itself is R. Hence, the resultant resistance of the circuit is $nR + R = ( n + 1 ) R$.



$∵ I = \dfrac{ε}{nR + R}$

⇒ $I = \dfrac{E}{( n + 1 ) R}$ .... (i)

In the case of parallel combination, these external n resistances are arranged in parallel,thereby their nett external resistance is $\dfrac{R}{n}$. This is in series with the internal resistance R.

Hence,

$10I$$= \dfrac{E}{\dfrac{R}{n} + R} = \dfrac{nE}{R + nR}$ .... (ii)

From (i) and (ii);

$n\dfrac{E}{R + nR} = 10\left(\dfrac{E}{nR + R}\right)$

$n = 10$

questions.q: The resistance of platinum wire at $0 ° C$ is $2Ω$ and $6 . 8Ω$ at $80 ° C$. The temperature coefficient of resistance of the wire is:
questions.solution:
The variation of resistance of a conducting metal with temperature is given by

${R}_{T} = {R}_{0}\left(1 + \alpha\left({T}_{2} - {T}_{1}\right)\right) . . . \left(1\right)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) and solve to calculate the required temperature coefficient.

$\begin{cases}6 . 8Ω & = & 2Ω \times \left(1 + \alpha\left(80 - 0\right) ° C\right) \\ ⇒ & 1 + 80\alpha = 3 . 4 \\ ⇒ & 80\alpha = 2 . 4 \\ ⇒ & \alpha = 3 \times {10}^{- 2}{C}^{- 1}\end{cases}$

questions.q: A filament bulb $( 500W, 100V )$ is to be used in a $230V$ main supply. When a resistance, $R$ is connected in series, it works perfectly and the bulb consumes $500W$. The value of $R$ is
questions.solution:
In the series, the current is the same in the bulb and the extra resistance, which is given by,

$I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{500}{100} = 5A$.

But, ${V}_{bulb} + {V}_{R} = {V}_{net}$.

So, voltage across resistance $R$ will be,

${V}_{R} = {V}_{net} - {V}_{bulb}$
$⇒ {V}_{R} = 230 - 100 = 130V$.

From Ohm's law,

$R = \dfrac{{V}_{R}}{I} = \dfrac{130}{5} = 26Ω$.

questions.q: The charge flowing through a resistance $\text{R}$ varies with time $t$ as $Q = at - bt^{2}$ where $\text{a}$ and $\text{b}$ are positive constants. The total heat produced in $\text{R}$ is:
questions.solution:
given

$Q = at - b{t}^{2}$

$i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = a - 2bt$

$i = 0$

at $\text{t} = \dfrac{\text{a}}{\text{2b}}$

$∴ dH = {i}^{2}Rdt$

$= {\left(a - 2bt\right)}^{2}Rdt$

$H = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{a}{2b}}{\left(a - 2bt\right)}^{2}Rdt$

${\left= \dfrac{{\left(a - 2bt\right)}^{3}R}{3\left(- 2b\right)}\right|}_{0}^{\dfrac{a}{2b}}$

$= \dfrac{1}{-6 b}\left[{\left(a - 2b\dfrac{a}{2b}\right)}^{3} - {\left(a\right)}^{3}\right]R$

$= - \dfrac{1}{6b}\left[{\left(0\right)}^{3} - {a}^{3}\right]R$

$\text{H} = \dfrac{{\text{a}}^{\text{3}} \text{R}}{6\text{b}}$

questions.q: Two cities are $150km$ apart. Electric power is sent from one city to another city through copper wires. The fall of potential per $km$ is $8$ volts and the average resistance per $km$ is $0.5Ω .$ The power loss in the wire is:
questions.solution:
Distance between the two cities, $150km$.

Voltage drop per kilometre is $8V{km}^{- 1}$.

Resistance per kilometre $0 . 5Ω{km}^{- 1}$

Total voltage drop will be,
${V}_{drop} = 150km \times 8V{km}^{- 1} = 1200V$

Total resistance of wire,
$R = 0.5Ω{km}^{- 1} \times 150km = 75Ω$

Therefore, the power loss will be, $P = \dfrac{{V}^{2}}{R} = \dfrac{{\left(150 \times 8\right)}^{2}}{0.5 \times 150} = 19.2kW$

questions.q:
Six similar bulbs are connected as shown in the figure with a DC source of emf $E$, and zero internal resistance.
The ratio of power consumption by the bulbs when $\left(i\right)$ all are glowing and $\left(ii\right)$ in the situation when two from section $A$ and one from section $B$ are glowing will be,
questions.solution:
Case (i): When all bulbs are glowing, then,

${R}_{eq} = \dfrac{2}{3}R$

Then, initially power consumption will be from the equation,

Power $P = \dfrac{{E}^{2}}{R}$

${P}_{i} = \dfrac{{E}^{2}}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{3{E}^{2}}{2R} . . . \left(1\right)$

Case (ii): When two bulbs in section $A$ and one bulb in the section are glowing,

${R}_{eq}^{'} = \dfrac{R}{2} + R = \dfrac{3}{2}R$
${P}_{f} = {E}^{2}{R}_{eq}^{'} = \dfrac{2{E}^{2}}{3R} . . . \left(2\right)$

From above two equations, ratio of power is,

$\dfrac{{P}_{i}}{{P}_{f}} = \dfrac{9}{4}$

questions.q: Two rods are joined to end, as shown. Both have a cross sectional area of 0.01 $\mathrm{cm}^2$. Each is 1 meter long. One rod is of copper with a resistivity of $17 \times 10^{-6}$ ohm-centimeter, the other is of iron with a resistivity of $10^{-5} \mathrm{ohm}$ centimeter. How much voltage is required to produce a current of 1 ampere in the rods?
questions.solution: According to the question Length of each $\operatorname{rod} l=1 \mathrm{~m}$ Area of cross-section of cach rod $\mathrm{A}=0.01 \mathrm{~cm}^2=0.01 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2\therefore$ If $\rho_{c u}=$ resistivity of copper and $\rho_{C W}$ is resistivity of iron then $\begin{aligned} & \rho_{c u}=1.7 \times 10^{-6} \Omega \mathrm{cm}=1.7 \times 10^{-8} \Omega \\ & \rho_{f e}=10^{-5} \Omega \mathrm{cm}=10^{-7} \Omega \end{aligned}$ New Resistance of $\mathrm{Cu}$ rod $=\mathrm{R}_{c u}= \begin{aligned} & \rho_{c u} \frac{1}{\mathrm{~A}} \\ & \text{$ and $Resistance of iron rod } \\ & \rho_{f e}=\rho_{f e} \frac{1}{\mathrm{~A}} \end{aligned}$ Both are connected in series then equivalent resistance is $\begin{aligned} R_{e s}=R_{c e}+R_{F e} & =\rho_{c u} \frac{l}{\mathrm{~A}}+\rho_{f e} \frac{l}{\mathrm{~A}}=\frac{l}{\mathrm{~A}} \\ \left(\rho_{c u}+\rho_{f e}\right) & \\ V & =I R \quad\{\text{ where } \mathrm{I}=1 \mathrm{~A}\} \\ & =I\left(R_{c u}+R_{f e}\right) \\ & =1\left(\rho_{c u}+\rho_{f e}\right) \\ & =\left(\rho_{c u}+\rho_{f e}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~A}}\right) \\ & =\left(1.7 \times 10^{-8}+10^{-7}\right) \\ & =10^{-7}(0.17+1)\left(10^6\right) \\ & =1.17 \times 10^{-1} \mathrm{~V} \\ & =0.117 \mathrm{~V} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: A $12 \mathrm{~cm}$ wire is given a shape of a right angled triangle $A B C$ having sides $3 \mathrm{~cm}$, $4 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $5 \mathrm{~cm}$ as shown in the figure. The resistance between two ends (AB, $B C, C A)$ of the respective sides are measured one by one by a multi-meter. The resistance will be in the ratio:
questions.solution:
Resistance of side $A B=R_1=\frac{3 \rho}{A}$ Resistance of side $B C=R_2=\frac{4 \rho}{A}$ Resistance of side $\mathrm{AC}=\mathrm{P}_3=\frac{5 \rho}{\mathrm{A}}$ (Where $A=$ Area of cross-section and $\rho=$ resistivity of wire)
$\therefore$ The resistance between $\mathrm{A} and \mathrm{B}$ is $\begin{aligned}$& $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{AB}}=\frac{R_1\left(R_2+R_3\right)}{R_1+R_2+R_3}=\frac{\frac{3 \rho}{A}\left(\frac{4 \rho}{A}+\frac{5 \rho}{A}\right)}{\frac{3 \rho}{A}+\frac{4 \rho}{A}+\frac{5 \rho}{A}}$\\ & =$\frac{27 \rho}{12 A}$\\ & $\text{ Similarly }$R_{B C}=$\frac{R_2\left(R_1+R_3\right)}{R_1+R_2+R_3}$\\ & $\frac{\frac{4 \rho}{A}\left(\frac{3 \rho}{A}+\frac{5 \rho}{A}\right)}{\frac{3 \rho}{A}+\frac{4 \rho}{A}+\frac{5 \rho}{A}}=\frac{32}{12} \frac{\rho}{A}$\\ & $\text{$ And }R_{A C}=$\frac{R_3\left(R_1+R_2\right)}{R_1+R_2+R_3}$\\ & =$\frac{\frac{5 \rho}{A}\left(\frac{3 \rho}{A}+\frac{3 \rho}{A}\right)}{\frac{5 \rho}{A}+\frac{3 \rho}{A}+\frac{4 \rho}{A}}=\frac{35}{12} \frac{\rho}{A}$\\ & \therefore R_{A B}: R_{B C}: R_{A C}=$\frac{27}{12}$: $\frac{32}{12}$: $\frac{35}{12}$\\ & =27: 32: 35 \\ & \end{aligned}

questions.q: A wire of resistance $4 \Omega$ is stretched to twice its original length. The resistance of stretched wire would be
questions.solution:
Let length and cross-section area of the wire be l and A respectively.
\(\therefore\) Resistance \(\mathrm{R}=\rho \frac{\mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{A}}\) where \(\rho\) is the resistivity of the material
Given: \(R=4 \Omega\)
For \(l^{\prime}=2 l\) and \(A^{\prime}=\frac{A}{2}\), resistance of the wire be \(R^{\prime}\)
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore R^{\prime}=\rho \frac{l^{\prime}}{A^{\prime}}=\rho \frac{2 l}{A / 2}=4 \rho \frac{1}{A}=4 R \\
& \therefore R^{\prime}=4 \times 4 \Omega=16 \Omega
\end{aligned}\)$

questions.q: If voltage across a bulb rated $220 \mathrm{~V}-100 \mathrm{~W}$ drops by $2.5 \%$ of its rated value, the percentage of the rated value by which the power would decrease is
questions.solution:
Power $P=\frac{V^2}{R}$
For small variation
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Delta P}{P} \times 100 \% & =\frac{2 \times \Delta V}{V} \times 100 \% \\
& =2 \times 2.5=5 \%
\end{aligned}$
Therefore, power would decrease by $5 \%$.

We knows $R \propto l$
Here, $\quad R_1+R_2=12 \Omega$
and $\quad \frac{R_1 \times R_2}{R_1+R_2}=\frac{8}{3} \Omega$
$\Rightarrow \quad R_1 R_2=32 \Omega$
We get, $R_1=8$ and $R_2=4$
Again, $R_1=\frac{12 l_1}{l_1+l_2}$
and $R_2=\frac{12 l_2}{l_1+l_2}$
Hence, $\quad \frac{l_1}{l_2}=\frac{1}{2}$

The potential gradient across the potentiometer wire, is $\mathrm{k}$ volt/cm and the ammeter, present in the circuit, reads 1.0 A when two way key is switched off. The balance points, when the key between the terminals (i) 1 and 2 (ii) 1 and 3 , is plugged in, are found to be at lengths $\mathrm{l}_1 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $\mathrm{l}_2 \mathrm{~cm}$ respectively. The magnitudes, of the resistors $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{X}$, in ohm, are then, equal, respectively, to
questions.solution:
The balancing length for $\mathrm{R}$ (when 1,2 are connected) be is $l_1$ and balancing length for $\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{X}$ (when 1,3 is connected is $\mathrm{l}_2$ )
Then $\quad \mathrm{iR}=\mathrm{kl}_1$
and $\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{X})=\mathrm{kl}_2$
Given $\quad \mathrm{i}=1 \mathrm{~A}$
$$
\begin{array}{r}
\mathrm{R}=\mathrm{kl}_1 \\
\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{kl}_2
\end{array}
$$
Subtracting Eq. (i) from Eq. (ii), we get
$$
\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{k}\left(\mathrm{l}_2-\mathrm{l}_1\right)
$$

A potentiometer circuit has been set up for finding the internal resistance of a given cell. The main battery, used across the potentiometer wire, has an emf of $2.0V$ and a negligible internal resistance. The potentiometer wire itself is $4m$ long. When the resistance, $R,$ connected across the given cell, has values of.
$\left(i\right)$ infinity $\left(ii\right)9.5Ω$
The 'balancing lengths, on the potentiometer wire are found to be $3m and 2.85m,$ respectively. The value of internal resistance of the cell is:
questions.solution:
Here, we have to calculate the internal resistence of the unknown cell.

So, we have to use the following formulae:

Internal resistance of the unknown cell is
$r = \left(\dfrac{{l}_{1}}{{l}_{2}} - 1\right)R = \left(\dfrac{3}{2.85} - 1\right)\left(9.5Ω\right) = 0.5Ω$

Hence the internal resistance will be 0.5 Ohm

questions.q: In an ammeter $0.2%$ of main current passes through the galvanometer. If resistance of galvanometer is $G,$ the resistance of ammeter will be:
questions.solution:
As shown in figure a shunt $S$ is connected in parallel with the galvanometer to convert it into the ammeter, let $G$ is the resistant of the galvanometer. Where $I$ is the current in the circuit as shown, according to question $0 \cdot 2 %$ current passing through the galvanometer, i.e.,

${I}_{G} = 0 \cdot 2 % ofI = \dfrac{0 \cdot 2}{100}I = \dfrac{I}{500}$;

so, the current through the shunt is $I = {I}_{G} + {I}_{S} ⇒ {I}_{S} = I - {I}_{G} ⇒ {I}_{S} = I - \dfrac{1}{500} = \dfrac{499}{500}I$
As $\left(G\right)$ and the shunt $\left(S\right)$ are in parallel combination ,

${V}_{G} = {V}_{S}$

${i}_{g}{R}_{g} = {i}_{s}{R}_{s} ⇒ \left(\dfrac{i}{500}\right)\left(G\right) = \left(\dfrac{499}{500}i\right)\left(S\right)$
$⇒ S = \dfrac{G}{499}$
Equivalent resistance of the ammeter
$\dfrac{1}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{G} + \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{G}{499}} ⇒ {R}_{eq} = \dfrac{G}{500}$

questions.q: A millivoltmeter of $25 \mathrm{mV}$ range is to be converted into an ammeter of 25 A range. The value (in ohm) of necessary shunt will be
questions.solution:
The full scale deflection current
$i_g=\frac{25 \mathrm{mV}}{G} \text{ ampere }$
where $G$ is the resistance of the meter.
The value of shunt required for converting it into ammeter of range $25 \mathrm{~A}$ is $S=\frac{i_g G}{i-i_g}$
So that, $S \approx \frac{25 \mathrm{mV}}{25}=0.001 \Omega$

questions.q: A wire of a certain material is stretched slowly by ten per cent. Its new resistance and specific resistance become respectively
questions.solution:
Key Idea : In stretching, specific resistance remains unchanged.
After stretching, specific resistance $(\rho)$ will remain same.
Original resistance of the wire,
$R=\frac{\rho l}{A} R \propto \frac{l}{A} \text{ or } R \propto \frac{l^2}{V}$ (as $V=A l$)
and $R^{\prime} \propto \frac{(l+10 \% l)^2}{V}$
Therefore, $\frac{R^{\prime}}{R}=\frac{\left(l+\frac{10}{100} l\right)^2}{l^2} \frac{R^{\prime}}{R}=\frac{\left(\frac{11 l}{10}\right)^2}{l^2}=\frac{121}{100} R^{\prime}=1.21 R$

questions.q: A cell can be balanced against $110 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $100 \mathrm{~cm}$ of potentiometer wire, respectively with and without being short circuited through a resistance of $10 \Omega$ Its internal resistance is
questions.solution:
Key Idea : This problem is based on the application of potentiometer in which we find the internal resistance of a cell.
In potentiometer experiment in which we find internal resistance of a cell, let $E$ be the emf of the cell and $V$ the terminal potential difference, then
$\frac{E}{V}=\frac{l_1}{l_2}$
where $l_1 and l_2$ are lengths of potentiometer wire with and without short circuited through a resistance.
Since, $\frac{E}{V}=\frac{R+r}{R}[\because E=I(R+r)$ and $V=I R] \therefore \frac{R+r}{R}=\frac{l_1}{l_2} \begin{aligned}
1+\frac{r}{R} & =\frac{110}{100} \\
\frac{r}{R} & =\frac{10}{100} \\
r & =\frac{1}{10} \times 10=1 \Omega
\end{aligned} r=\frac{1}{10} \times 10=1 \Omega$

questions.solution: The bridge formed with given resistances is a balanced Wheatstone's bridge The situation can be depicted as shown in the figure. questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The \(V-I\) graph for a conductor at temperature \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are as shown in the figure. \(T_2-T_1\) is proportional to
questions.solution:
\(V-I\) graph for conductor at temperature \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) is shown in the figure.

We know that resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to its temperature.
\($\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Hence, } & R_1 \propto T_1 \Rightarrow \tan \theta \propto T_1 \\
\Rightarrow & \tan \theta=K T_1 \quad \ldots (i) \\
\text{and } & R_2 \propto T_2 \\
\Rightarrow & \tan \left(90^{\circ}-\theta\right) \propto T_2 \\
\Rightarrow & \cot \theta \propto T_2 \\
\Rightarrow & \cot \theta=K T_2 \quad \ldots (ii)
\end{array}$\(\therefore\) From $Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get\begin{aligned}
& K T_2-K T_1=\cot \theta-\tan \theta \\
& K\left(T_2-T_1\right)=\frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}-\frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \\
& \Rightarrow T_2-T_1=\frac{\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta}{K \sin \theta \cos \theta} \\
& \Rightarrow T_2-T_1=\frac{\cos 2 \theta}{\frac{1}{2} \sin 2 \theta} \Rightarrow T_2-T_1=\frac{2 \cot 2 \theta}{K} \\
& \Rightarrow T_2-T_1 \propto \cot 2 \theta \\
\end{aligned}\)$

An infinite line charge of uniform electric charge density $\lambda$ lies along the axis of an electrically conducting infinite cylindrical shell of radius R. At time t = 0, the space inside the cylinder is filled with a material of permittivity $ε$ and electrical conductivity $\sigma$ . The electrical conduction in the material follows Ohm's law.
Which one of the following graphs best describes the subsequent variation of the magnitude of current density j(t) at any point in the material?
questions.solution:
This is the problem of RC circuit where the product RC is a constant.
So, due to leakage current, charge and current density will exponentially decay and will infinite time. So correct answer is A
For any small element
Resistance R = $\dfrac{dr}{\sigma\left(2\pirl\right)}$
Capacitance C $= \dfrac{ϵ2\pirl}{dr}$
Product $R \times C = \dfrac{ϵ}{\sigma} =$ constant
$q = {q}_{0}{e}^{- \left(\dfrac{t\sigma}{ϵ}\right)}$
$I = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \dfrac{{q}_{0}\sigma}{ϵ}{e}^{- \left(\dfrac{t\sigma}{ϵ}\right)}$
Current density $= \dfrac{I}{A} = \dfrac{{q}_{0}\dfrac{\sigma}{ϵ}{e}^{- \dfrac{t\sigma}{ϵ}}}{2\pirl}$
$j\infty{e}^{- \dfrac{t\sigma}{ϵ}}$

questions.q: $I-V$ characteristic of a copper wire of length $L$ and area of cross-section $A$ is shown in figure. The slope of the curve becomes
options: More if experiment is performed at higher temperature
More if a wire of steel of same dimension is used
Less if the area of the wire is increased
Less if the length of the wire is increased
questions.solution:
$I-V$ characteristics of copper wire of length $L$ and area of cross-section $A$ is shown in the figure.

Since, $I-V$ characteristic is a straight line, hence it obeys $\mathrm{Ohm}^{\prime}$ s law. According to which resistance of copper wire, $\begin{aligned} R &=\frac{V}{I}=\cot \theta \\ \Rightarrow \quad R &=\cot \theta \\ \Rightarrow \quad \rho \cdot \frac{l}{A} &=\cot \theta \end{aligned}$ or $\quad \tan \theta \propto\left(\frac{A}{\rho l}\right)$ Hence, slope $(\tan \theta)$ of the curve becomes (i) less if the length of the wire is increased. (ii) more if the area of the wire is increased. (iii) less if a wire of steel of same dimensions is used as $\rho_{\text{steel }}>\rho_{\text{copper }}$. (iv) less if experiment is performed at higher temperature.

questions.q:
Assertion (A) When a wire of aluminium and another wire of silicon are heated from room temperature to $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the conductivity of aluminium increases and that of silicon decreases.

Reason (R) Aluminium has positive temperature coefficient of resistivity and silicon has negative temperature coefficient of resistivity.
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct.
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct.
questions.solution:
Key Idea In nature, metals have positive
temperature coefficient and semiconductors have negative temperature coefficient.

Aluminium is a metal, so its conductivity decreases with increase in temperature, due to the excessive collision of electron. Whereas, $\mathrm{Si}$ is a semiconductor therefore its conductivity increases with increase in temperature.

All metals have positive temperature coefficient of resistivity and semiconductor has negative temperature coefficient of resistivity. Hence, assertion (A) is incorrect but reason (R) is correct.

questions.q:
Choose the correct option with respect to the statements $A$ and $B$
(A):When no electric field is applied across a conductor, the path of free electrons between two successive collisions in it is straight
(B): When an electric field is applied across a conductor, the drift velocity of electrons is independent of time
options: A is true and B is false
A is false and B is true
questions.solution:
- (A): In absence of electric field, electrons move freely between collisions \(\rightarrow\) path is straight. \(\sim\) True
- (B): In presence of electric field, electrons acquire a constant average drift velocity (\(v_d=\frac{e E \tau}{m}\)), which does not change with time. \(\checkmark\) True
Hence, both A and B are true.

Statement 1: $\mathrm{In}$ a Meter Bridge experiment, null point for an unknown resistance is measured. Now, the unknown resistance is put inside an enclosure maintained at a higher temperature. The null point can be obtained at the same point as before by decreasing the value of the standard resistance.
and Statement 2: Resistance of a metal increase with increase in temperature.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
With increase in temperature, the value of unknown resistance will increase.
In balanced Wheatstone bridge condition, $\frac{R}{X}=\frac{l_1}{l_2}$
Here, $R=$ value of standard resistance,
$X=$ value of unknown resistance .
To take null point at same point or $\frac{l_1}{l_2}$ to remain unchanged, $\frac{R}{X}$ should also remain unchanged. Therefore, if $X$ is increasing $R$ should also increase.
$\therefore$ correct option is (d).

Given below are two statements:

Statement I : The equivalent resistance of resistors in a series combination is smaller than least resistance used in the combination.

Statement II : The resistivity of the material is independent of temperature. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are false
Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are true
Statement $I$ is true but Statement $II$ is false
Statement $I$ is false but Statement $II$ is true
questions.solution:
The formula for series equivalent resistance is given by 

${R}_{s} = {R}_{1} + {R}_{2} + . . . . . . + {R}_{n}$. 

Hence, the equivalent resistance will be the highest value compared to other resistances.

The resistivity of a material is given by,

$ρ = {ρ}^{0}\left(1 + \alpha\DeltaT\right)$

Clearly, the resistivity is dependant on temperature.

Hence, this is the right option.

Statement (I) : Specific resistance depends on nature of material and independent of temperature of the material.
Statement (II) : A wire of resistance $6 \Omega$ is drawn out so that its new length is four times its original length. The resistance of the new wire is $48 \Omega$.
Statement (III) : Drift velocity is the average constant velocity acquired by free electrons inside a metal by the application of an electric field which results in current. 
Which of the following is correct?
options: Statements I, II and III are true
Statement I is true, but statements II, III is false
Statement III is true, but statements I, II are false
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false
questions.solution:
Specific resistance depends both on temperature and nature of material.
So (I) is incorrect.
When length becomes ' $n$ ' time, resistance becomes $n^2$ times. So new resistance will be $4^2 \times 6=96 \Omega$
So (II) is incorrect.
Drift velocity is average velocity with which free electron get drifted in direction of electric field.
So (III) is correct.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : In balanced Wheatstone bridge, the current through cell depends on resistance of galvanometer.
Reason (R) : At balanced condition current through galvanometer is zero.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): "In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the current through the cell depends on the resistance of the galvanometer." This is false. In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the current through the cell depends on the external resistances, but the galvanometer has no current when the bridge is balanced. Therefore, the galvanometer's resistance does not affect the current through the cell in this condition.

Assertion (A) : In series combination of electrical bulb, lower power rating bulb emits more light than that of higher power rating bulb.
Reason (R) : The lower power rating bulb in series gets more current than the higher power rating bulb.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): In a series combination of electrical bulbs, the bulb with the lower power rating will have a higher resistance, and in a series circuit, the current is the same through all components. Since the lower power bulb has a higher resistance, it will dissipate more power (\(P=I^2 R\)), meaning it will emit more light than the higher power rating bulb. So, Assertion (A) is true.
- Reason (R): In a series circuit, the current is the same for all components. Hence, it is incorrect to say that the lower power bulb gets more current than the higher power rating bulb. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : When an extemal resistor of resistance R (connected across a cell of internal resistance r) is varied, power consumed by resistance \(R\) is maximum when \(R=r\).
Reason (R) : Power consumed by a resistor of constant resistance R is maximum when current through it is maximum.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): The power consumed by an external resistor \(R\) connected to a cell of internal resistance \(r\) is maximum when \(R=\). This is known as the condition for maximum power transfer, where the external resistance is equal to the internal resistance of the power source. So, Assertion (A) is true.
- Reason (R): Power consumed by a resistor is not necessarily maximum when the current through it is maximum. In fact, if the current is maximum, that typically means \(R\) is very small, leading to lower power consumption (since \(P=I^2 R\)). The maximum power occurs when \(R=r\), not when the current is at its maximum. Hence, Reason (R) is false.

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Ohm's law holds only for small currents in metallic wire not for high currents.
Reason (R) : For metallic wire resistance increases with increase in temperature. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
questions.solution:
- Assertion (A): Ohm's law holds only for small currents in metallic wire, not for high currents.
- This is incorrect. Ohm's law, \(V=I R\), holds as long as the material remains ohmic (i.e., the resistance is constant). It can hold for both small and large currents, provided the temperature and material properties remain unchanged. Large currents may cause heating, which can lead to a change in resistance, but this does not mean Ohm's law is inherently limited to small currents.
- Reason (R): For metallic wire, resistance increases with an increase in temperature.
- This is correct. In metallic conductors, resistance typically increases with temperature due to increased collisions between charge carriers and atoms.

questions.q:
Statement 1: Voltage across a battery is always less than its emf. and
Statement 2 : There is always some loss of energy due to internal resistance of the battery.
options: Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True ; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement- 1 is True, Statement- 2 is True ; Statement-2 is not a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement- 1 is True, Statement- 2 is False.
Statement- 1 is False, Statement- 2 is True.
questions.solution:
- Statement 1: Voltage across a battery is always less than its emf.
- This is true in most practical scenarios. The terminal voltage \(V\) of a battery is given by \(V=\mathrm{emf}-I r\), where \(I\) is the current and \(r\) is the internal resistance. When current flows through the circuit, some voltage drop occurs across the internal resistance, making the terminal voltage less than the emf. If no current flows, the terminal voltage is equal to the emf. Therefore, the statement holds true for real batteries under load.
- Statement 2: There is always some loss of energy due to the internal resistance of the battery.
- This is true. When current flows, some energy is dissipated as heat in the internal resistance, which results in energy loss.

questions.q:
Statement-1 : In real battery total chemical energy lost in the battery can not be obtained at load resistance.
and
Statement-2 : Two heaters with different resistance are connected in parallel. Higher resistance heater will glow more.
options: Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is not a correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is False.
Statement-1 is False, Statement-2 is True.
questions.solution:
- Statement 1: In a real battery, total chemical energy lost in the battery cannot be obtained at the load resistance.
- This is true. In real batteries, some energy is always lost due to internal resistance as heat, so not all the chemical energy is delivered to the external circuit (load resistance). Therefore, the total chemical energy cannot be fully transferred to the load.
- Statement 2: Two heaters with different resistance are connected in parallel. The higher resistance heater will glow more.
- This is false. When resistors (or heaters) are connected in parallel, the voltage across each is the same. The power dissipated in each heater is given by \(P=\frac{V^2}{R}\). For a higher resistance heater, the power will be lower compared to the lower resistance heater because power is inversely proportional to resistance. Thus, the lower resistance heater will glow more, not the higher resistance one.
Conclusion:
The correct option is:
(3) Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is False.

A. The drift velocity of electrons decreases with the increase in the temperature of conductor.
B. The drift velocity is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section of given conductor.
C. The drift velocity does not depend on the applied potential difference to the conductor.
D. The drift velocity of electron is inversely proportional to the length of the conductor.
E. The drift velocity increases with the increase in the temperature of conductor.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Drift velocity $= \left(\dfrac{eτ}{m}\right)E$

${v}_{d} = \left(\dfrac{eτ}{m}\right)\left(\dfrac{\DeltaV}{l}\right)$

$\DeltaV =$ Potential difference applied across the wire As temperature increases, relaxation time decreases, hence ${V}_{d}$ decreases.
As per formula, ${V}_{d} ∝ \dfrac{1}{l}$

${v}_{d} = \dfrac{I}{neA}$, as it is not mentioned that current is at steady state neither it is mentioned that $n$ is constant for given conductor. So it can't be said that ${v}_{d}$ is inversely proportional to $A$.

$I = neA{v}_{d} = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{V}{ρl}A$

${v}_{d} = \dfrac{eEτ}{m}$

$τ$ decrease with temperature increase.

First and fourth statements are correct.

${v}_{d} = \dfrac{V}{ρlne}\left(E = \dfrac{V}{l}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements :
Statement I : A uniform wire of resistance $80Ω$ is cut into four equal parts. These parts are now connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance of the combination will be $5Ω$.

Statement II : Two resistance $2R$ and $3R$ are connected in parallel in an electric circuit. The value of thermal energy developed in $3R$ and $2R$ will be in the ratio $3: 2$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both statement I and statement II are correct
Both statement I and statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct.
questions.solution:
Statement $1 -$ $R = 80Ω$

When it is cut into $4$ equal parts, the resistance of each part will be,

${R}_{1} = {R}_{2} = {R}_{3} = {R}_{4} = 20Ω$

When these resistances are connected in parallel,

${R}_{eq} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5Ω$

Hence, the statement I is correct.

Statement 2 -

When the resistances are connected in parallel, the potential difference between them is same. Therefore, the power consumed can be written as,

$P = \dfrac{{V}^{2}}{R}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{P}_{1}}{{P}_{2}} = \left(\dfrac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1}}\right) = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Hence, statement II is incorrect.

$S = \dfrac{{I}_{g}G}{I - {I}_{g}} ⇒ S = \dfrac{{10}^{- 3} \times 54}{( 10 - 1 ) \times {10}^{- 3}} = 6Ω$

questions.q:
Consider an electrical conductor connected across a potential difference $V$. Let $\Delta q$ be a small charge moving through it in time $\Delta t$. If $I$ is the electric current through it,
I. the kinetic energy of the charge increases by $I V \Delta t$.
II. the electric potential energy of the charge decreases by $I V \Delta t$.
III. the thermal energy of the conductor increases by IV $\Delta t$.
Choose the correct option.
questions.solution:
As the charges flow from higher potential to lower potential.
So, its potential energy decreases by $I V \Delta t$ but kinetic energy increase.
This increase in energy is transferred to conductor which increases the thermal energy by $I V \Delta t$.
So, statements (II) and (III) are correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A student in a town in India, where the price per unit (1 unit $= 1kWh$ ) of electricity is $₹ 5 . 00,$ purchases a $1kVA$ UPS (uninterrupted power supply) battery. A day before the exam, 10 friends arrive to the student's home with their laptops and all connect their laptops to the UPS. Assume that each laptop has a constant power requirement of $90W$. Consider the following statements.
I. All the 10 laptops can be powered by the UPS, if connected directly.
II. All the 10 laptops can be powered, if connected using an extension box with a 3 A fuse.
III. If all the 10 friends use the laptop for $5h$, then the cost of the consumed electricity is about $₹ 22 . 50 .$
Select the correct option with the true statements.
questions.solution:
Power requirement for 1 laptop, ${P}_{1} = 90W$
So, power r quirement for 10 laptops,
$\begin{array}{ll}P = 10 \times {P}_{1} = 10 \times 90 \\ - 900W = 0 . 9kW\end{array}$
In $5h,$ electrical energy used by all laptops,

$E = P \times t = 0 . 9 \times 5$

$= 4 . 5kWh$

cost of electrical energy used is
cost $= E \times$ Unit cost

$= 4 . 5 \times 5$
$= ₹ 22 . 50$

So, statement III is correct.
For laptop charger, input voltage is $220V$
So, current when all 10 laptops are connected through an extension,

$I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{900}{220} \approx 4 . 1A$

As, line current exceeds current rating of fuse, therefore $3A$ fuse cannot be used. So, statement II is incorrect.

B) Electric field exerts force on both stationary and moving charge

So only $\left(A\right) \text{$ and }$\left(B\right) is correct.$

Statement (I) : The temperature coefficient of resistance for most of meals in pure form is positive.
Statement (II) : A metal wire $2 \mathrm{~mm}$ in diameter carries a charge of $360 \pi \mathrm{C}$ in two hours. If the metal contains $5 \times 10^{22}$ free electrons $/ \mathrm{cm}^3$, then drift velocity of the electrons in the wire is $6.25 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
Statement (III) : Semiconductors like pure germanium does not obey Ohm's law for all range of electric field values. Which of the following is correct?
options: Statements I, II, III are true.
Statements I, II are true, but statement III is false.
Statements II, III are true, but statement I is false.
Statements I, II, III are false.
questions.solution:
For all metal, temperature coefficient is always positive
So (I) is true
We have
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{neA}}=\frac{\frac{360 \pi}{7200}}{5 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times \pi \times\left(1 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2} \\
& =6.25 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
So, (II) is true
Only metals obey ohm law therefore (III) is correct.

questions.q:
Two heaters designed for the same voltage V have different power ratings. When connected individually across a source of voltage \(V\), they produce H amount of heat each in times \($\mathrm{t}}_{1}\) and \( \mathrm{t}$}_{2}\) respectively. When used together across the same source, they produce H amount of heat in time \(t\). Then correct option is
(a) If they are in series, \(t=t_1+t_2\)
(b) If they are in series, \(t=2$\left($t_1+t_2\right)\)
(c) If they are in parallel, \(t=$\frac{t_1 t_2}{\left(t_1+t_2\right)}$\)
(d) If they are in parallel, \(t=$\frac{t_1 t_2}{2\left(t_1+t_2\right)}$\)
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \frac{\mathrm{V}^2}{\mathrm{R}} \mathrm{t}=\text{ constant } \\ & \therefore \mathrm{t} \propto \mathrm{R} \\ & \text{$ In $series } \quad \mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{s}}=\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2 \\ & \text{ In parallel } \quad \mathrm{t}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{t}_1 \mathrm{t}_2}{\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2}\end{aligned}\)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
If the current in resistance of uniform cross section is doubled then, (assume temperature to be approximately constant).
(A) the current density is doubled
(B) the conduction electron density is doubled
(C) the mean time between collision is constant
(D) the electron drift speed is doubled
questions.solution:
- (A) The current density is doubled:
- Current density \(J\) is given by \(J=\frac{I}{A}\), where \(I\) is the current and \(A\) is the cross-sectional area. If the current \(I\) is doubled and the cross-sectional area \(A\) remains constant, then the current density will also double. This statement is true.
- (B) The conduction electron density is doubled:
- The conduction electron density refers to the number of free electrons per unit volume in the material, which is a property of the material and does not change with the current. Therefore, this statement is false.

Current \(i\) is flowing through a wire of nonuniform cross section as shown. Match the following two columns. \(
Column-IColumn-II

questions.solution:
Let's break down the problem and match Column-I with Column-II:
- (a) Current density: Current density \(J=$\frac{I}{A}$\), where \(I\) is the current and \(A\) is the cross-sectional area. In a wire with non-uniform cross section, the current density will be greater where the cross-sectional area is smaller. Therefore, the current density is more at section 1 if section 1 has a smaller cross-sectional area compared to section 2.
- So, (a) matches (p).
- (b) Electric field: The electric field \(E\) in a conductor is related to the current density by \(J=$\sigma$E\), where \($\sigma$\) is the conductivity. Since current density is higher in the narrower section, the electric field will also be higher there. Thus, the electric field is more at section 1 if section 1 has a smaller cross-sectional area.
So, (b) matches (q).
- (c) Resistance per unit length: The resistance per unit length is given by \(R=$\frac{\rho}{A}$\), where \(\rho\) is the resistivity and \(A\) is the cross-sectional area. If the wire has different cross-sectional areas at sections 1 and 2, the resistance per unit length will be different. If the cross-sectional area changes, the resistance will also change.
- So, (c) does not have enough data to determine this, as it depends on the cross-sectional areas of sections 1 and 2.
- (c) matches (s).
- (d) Potential difference per unit length: The potential difference per unit length \(V / L\) is related to the electric field by \(E=V / L\). If the electric field is different in sections 1 and 2 (as implied in part b), the potential difference per unit length will also differ. So, potential difference per unit length should be different if the cross-sectional area varies.
- So, (d) matches (p).
Conclusion:
The correct matching is:
(4) a-p, b-q, c-r, d-s.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): If the resistance of every individual resistor in an infinite ladder network is doubled, the overall equivalent resistance of the network is also doubled.
Reason (R): The equivalent resistance of an infinite ladder network is determined by solving a quadratic equation.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is correct. In any purely linear resistive network, scaling all constituent resistors by a factor $k$ scales the overall equivalent resistance by the same factor $k$. Thus, doubling all individual resistances doubles the equivalent resistance.

Reason (R) is also correct. The standard method to find the equivalent resistance of an infinite ladder is to assume the resistance of the infinite network is $R_{eq}$, and then set up an equation by adding one repeating unit to $R_{eq}$, which results in a quadratic equation in terms of $R_{eq}$.

However, (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). The fact that the equivalent resistance doubles is due to the linear nature of Ohm's law and resistive networks, not merely because it is solved via a quadratic equation. Therefore, both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.q: Two resistors, $X$ and $Y$, are connected in parallel across a constant DC voltage source. A graph of the thermal energy ($H$) developed in each resistor versus time ($t$) is plotted. The graph yields two straight lines passing through the origin, where the line for resistor $X$ is steeper than the line for resistor $Y$. Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between their resistances, $R_X$ and $R_Y$?
options: The relationship cannot be determined without knowing the applied voltage
questions.solution:
In a parallel circuit, the potential difference ($V$) across both resistors is the same.

The thermal energy produced in a resistor in time $t$ is given by $H = \dfrac{V^2}{R}t$.

For a graph of $H$ versus $t$, the slope of the line is $\dfrac{H}{t} = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$.

Since the line for resistor $X$ is steeper than the line for resistor $Y$, the slope for $X$ is greater than the slope for $Y$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{V^2}{R_X} > \dfrac{V^2}{R_Y}$.

Since $V^2$ is constant and positive, this inequality simplifies to $R_X < R_Y$.

Assuming $R_X > R_Y$ is a common mistake that occurs if one incorrectly applies the series heating formula ($H = I^2Rt$) to a parallel combination.

Answer: $R_X < R_Y$

questions.q: The variation of terminal voltage $V$ with current $I$ drawn from a discharging cell is plotted as a straight line graph. The line intersects the $V$-axis at $1.5$ V and the $I$-axis at $3.0$ A. The emf and internal resistance of the cell are respectively :
questions.solution:
For a discharging cell, the terminal voltage is given by the equation:

$V = E - Ir$

When the current $I = 0$, the terminal voltage equals the emf ($E$) of the cell. The graph intersects the $V$-axis at $1.5$ V, which represents the open-circuit condition. Thus, $E = 1.5$ V.

When the terminal voltage $V = 0$, the current is the short-circuit current, $I_{max} = \dfrac{E}{r}$. The graph intersects the $I$-axis at $3.0$ A.

Therefore, the internal resistance $r$ is:

$r = \dfrac{E}{I_{max}} = \dfrac{1.5}{3.0} = 0.5\ \Omega$

Answer: $1.5$ V, $0.5\ \Omega$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Two resistors having equal initial resistance $R_0$ at a reference temperature, one with a positive temperature coefficient of resistance ($+\alpha$) and the other with a negative temperature coefficient ($-\alpha$), are connected in parallel. As the temperature of the combination increases, their equivalent resistance remains constant.

Reason (R): For these two resistors, the sum of their resistances is independent of temperature, whereas the product of their resistances decreases with an increase in temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true
questions.solution:
Let the resistances at an increased temperature be $R_1 = R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$ and $R_2 = R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T)$.

The sum of the resistances is:
$R_1 + R_2 = R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T) + R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T) = 2R_0$
This sum is independent of the temperature change.

The product of the resistances is:
$R_1 R_2 = R_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T) \times R_0(1 - \alpha \Delta T) = R_0^2(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)$
As temperature increases ($\Delta T$ increases), the term $(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)$ decreases, so the product of the resistances decreases. Thus, the Reason (R) is true.

The equivalent resistance in parallel is given by:
$R_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = \dfrac{R_0^2(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)}{2R_0} = \dfrac{R_0}{2}(1 - \alpha^2 \Delta T^2)$
Since the product decreases while the sum remains constant, the equivalent resistance $R_{\text{eq}}$ decreases with an increase in temperature. Therefore, the Assertion (A) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true

questions.q: A battery of EMF $18\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $2\ \Omega$ is connected in a single closed loop with another battery of EMF $6\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1\ \Omega$. The two batteries are connected in opposition. An external resistor of $9\ \Omega$ is also connected in series in the loop. What is the potential difference across the terminals of the $6\text{ V}$ battery?
questions.solution:
The two batteries are connected in opposition, so their net EMF is the difference between their individual EMFs:
$E_{\text{net}} = 18\text{ V} - 6\text{ V} = 12\text{ V}$.

The total resistance in the circuit is the sum of the external resistance and the internal resistances of both batteries:
$R_{\text{net}} = 9\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega + 1\ \Omega = 12\ \Omega$.

The current in the circuit is:
$I = \dfrac{E_{\text{net}}}{R_{\text{net}}} = \dfrac{12}{12} = 1\text{ A}$.

Since the $18\text{ V}$ battery dominates, the current flows out of its positive terminal and enters the positive terminal of the $6\text{ V}$ battery. This means the $6\text{ V}$ battery is being charged.

For a battery being charged, the terminal potential difference $V$ is given by:
$V = E + Ir$

Substituting the values for the $6\text{ V}$ battery:
$V = 6 + (1)(1) = 7\text{ V}$.

Answer: $7\text{ V}$

$E_{\text{net}} = 18\text{ V} - 6\text{ V} = 12\text{ V}$.

The total resistance in the circuit is the sum of the external resistance and the internal resistances of both batteries:
$R_{\text{net}} = 9\ \Omega + 2\ \Omega + 1\ \Omega = 12\ \Omega$.

The current in the circuit is:
$I = \dfrac{E_{\text{net}}}{R_{\text{net}}} = \dfrac{12}{12} = 1\text{ A}$.

Since the $18\text{ V}$ battery dominates, the current flows out of its positive terminal and enters the positive terminal of the $6\text{ V}$ battery. This means the $6\text{ V}$ battery is being charged.

For a battery being charged, the terminal potential difference $V$ is given by:
$V = E + Ir$

Substituting the values for the $6\text{ V}$ battery:
$V = 6 + (1)(1) = 7\text{ V}$.

Answer: $7\text{ V}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cell of emf $6 \mathrm{~V}$ and internal resistance $1 \Omega$ is connected across a parallel combination of two identical external resistors of $4 \Omega$ each. The terminal potential difference of the cell is:
questions.solution:
The equivalent resistance of the two $4 \Omega$ resistors in parallel is:
$R_{\text{eq}} = \dfrac{4 \times 4}{4 + 4} = 2 \Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit, including the internal resistance $r$, is:
$R_{\text{total}} = R_{\text{eq}} + r = 2 + 1 = 3 \Omega$

The current drawn from the cell is:
$i = \dfrac{E}{R_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2 \mathrm{~A}$

The terminal potential difference $V$ across the cell is the voltage across the equivalent external resistance:
$V = i \times R_{\text{eq}} = 2 \times 2 = 4 \mathrm{~V}$

Alternatively, using the cell formula:
$V = E - ir = 6 - (2 \times 1) = 4 \mathrm{~V}$

Answer: $4 \mathrm{~V}$

questions.q: Ten identical cells, each of emf $2\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $0.5\ \Omega$, are connected in series to form a battery. However, two of the cells are connected with reverse polarity. If this battery is connected across an external resistor of $5\ \Omega$, the steady current flowing through the circuit will be
questions.solution:
Total number of cells, $n = 10$

Number of reversed cells, $m = 2$

When $m$ cells are reversed out of $n$ cells, the effective emf of the series combination is given by:
$E_{\text{eff}} = (n - 2m)E = (10 - 2 \times 2) \times 2\text{ V} = 6 \times 2\text{ V} = 12\text{ V}$

The internal resistance of the cells is independent of their polarity. Thus, the total internal resistance is:
$r_{\text{eq}} = n \times r = 10 \times 0.5\ \Omega = 5\ \Omega$

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of the external resistance $R$ and the equivalent internal resistance $r_{\text{eq}}$:
$R_{\text{total}} = R + r_{\text{eq}} = 5\ \Omega + 5\ \Omega = 10\ \Omega$

According to Ohm's law, the steady current $I$ is:
$I = \dfrac{E_{\text{eff}}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{12}{10}\text{ A} = 1.2\text{ A}$

Answer: $1.2\text{ A}$

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For the most precise measurement of an unknown resistance using a Wheatstone bridge, the ratio arms should be small and approximately equal to each other.

Reason (R): Small and equal ratio arms ensure a large galvanometer deflection even for a very small unbalance in the bridge circuit.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion
Assertion is correct but Reason is incorrect
Assertion is incorrect but Reason is correct
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) states that for precise measurement, the ratio arms should be small and approximately equal. This is correct because the sensitivity of a Wheatstone bridge is maximum when all four arms have resistances of the same order of magnitude. Furthermore, smaller overall resistances allow a larger current to flow from the battery.

Reason (R) states that this ensures a large galvanometer deflection for a small unbalance. This is also correct. The precision of the measurement depends on how easily a slight unbalance can be detected. A larger current leads to a larger deflection in the galvanometer for the same fractional change in resistance, making it easier to find the exact null point.

Thus, both Assertion and Reason are correct, and the Reason correctly explains the physical mechanism behind the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Ten identical cells, each of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected in series and the combination is short-circuited by a thick wire of zero resistance. The steady current in the circuit is $I_s$. The same ten cells are then connected in parallel and the combination is similarly short-circuited, producing a steady current $I_p$. The ratio $\dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$ is:
questions.solution:
When $10$ identical cells of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ are connected in series, the equivalent emf is $10E$ and the equivalent internal resistance is $10r$.

The short-circuit current $I_s$ is given by:
$I_s = \dfrac{10E}{10r} = \dfrac{E}{r}$

When the same $10$ cells are connected in parallel, the equivalent emf remains $E$ and the equivalent internal resistance becomes $\dfrac{r}{10}$.

The short-circuit current $I_p$ is given by:
$I_p = \dfrac{E}{\dfrac{r}{10}} = \dfrac{10E}{r}$

The required ratio is:
$\dfrac{I_p}{I_s} = \dfrac{\dfrac{10E}{r}}{\dfrac{E}{r}} = 10$

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A Wheatstone bridge has four arms with resistances $P = 10 \, \Omega$, $Q = 20 \, \Omega$, $R = 15 \, \Omega$, and $S$ being a metallic coil. The bridge is initially balanced at $20^\circ\text{C}$. The temperature of the coil $S$ is then raised to $120^\circ\text{C}$. If the temperature coefficient of resistance of the coil's material is $5 \times 10^{-3} \, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$, what value of shunt resistance must be connected in parallel with the heated coil to restore the balance of the bridge?
questions.solution:
For the bridge to be balanced initially, $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S_0}$.

Substituting the given values: $\dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{15}{S_0} \Rightarrow S_0 = 30 \, \Omega$.

When the temperature of the coil is raised, its new resistance $S'$ is given by:
$S' = S_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$
$S' = 30 [1 + 5 \times 10^{-3} \times (120 - 20)]$
$S' = 30 [1 + 0.5] = 45 \, \Omega$.

To restore the balance, the equivalent resistance of this arm must be brought back to $30 \, \Omega$. Since $45 \, \Omega > 30 \, \Omega$, a shunt resistance $R_x$ must be connected in parallel.

$\dfrac{1}{S'} + \dfrac{1}{R_x} = \dfrac{1}{S_0}$
$\dfrac{1}{45} + \dfrac{1}{R_x} = \dfrac{1}{30}$
$\dfrac{1}{R_x} = \dfrac{1}{30} - \dfrac{1}{45} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{90} = \dfrac{1}{90}$

$\Rightarrow R_x = 90 \, \Omega$.

Answer: $90 \, \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A storage battery of emf $8\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $0.5\ \Omega$ is being charged by a $12\text{ V}$ DC supply using a series resistor of $3.5\ \Omega$. What is the terminal voltage of the battery during the charging process?
questions.solution:
During the charging of a battery, the positive terminal of the DC supply is connected to the positive terminal of the battery. The net emf in the circuit is the difference between the supply voltage and the battery emf.

Net emf $= 12\text{ V} - 8\text{ V} = 4\text{ V}$

Total resistance in the circuit $= R + r = 3.5\ \Omega + 0.5\ \Omega = 4\ \Omega$

Charging current $I = \dfrac{\text{Net emf}}{\text{Total resistance}} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1\text{ A}$

During charging, the current enters the positive terminal of the battery. Therefore, the terminal voltage ($V$) is greater than its emf ($E$).

$V = E + Ir = 8 + (1 \times 0.5) = 8.5\text{ V}$

Answer: $8.5\text{ V}$

questions.q: A storage battery of emf $6 \text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1 \Omega$ is being charged by a $30 \text{ V}$ DC supply using a series resistor of $5 \Omega$. What is the terminal potential difference across the battery during the charging process?
questions.solution:
During charging, the DC supply opposes the emf of the battery. The net emf in the circuit is:
$E_{\text{net}} = V_{\text{supply}} - E = 30 - 6 = 24 \text{ V}$

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of the series resistor and the internal resistance of the battery:
$R_{\text{total}} = R + r = 5 + 1 = 6 \Omega$

The charging current $i$ in the circuit is:
$i = \dfrac{E_{\text{net}}}{R_{\text{total}}} = \dfrac{24}{6} = 4 \text{ A}$

When a battery is being charged, the current enters its positive terminal. The terminal potential difference $V$ across the battery is given by:
$V = E + ir$
$V = 6 + (4 \times 1) = 10 \text{ V}$

Answer: $10 \text{ V}$

questions.q: An infinite ladder network is constructed using repeating L-sections. Each L-section consists of a series resistor of $1\ \Omega$ and a parallel (shunt) resistor of $2\ \Omega$. This infinite network is connected across a battery of EMF $12\ \text{V}$ and unknown internal resistance $r$. If the total steady current drawn from the battery is $4\ \text{A}$, the value of $r$ is:
questions.solution:
Let the equivalent resistance of the infinite ladder network be $R$.
Since adding one more L-section to an infinite ladder does not change its equivalent resistance, we can write:
$R = 1 + \dfrac{2R}{2 + R}$
$\Rightarrow R(2 + R) = 2 + R + 2R$
$\Rightarrow 2R + R^2 = 3R + 2$
$\Rightarrow R^2 - R - 2 = 0$
$\Rightarrow (R - 2)(R + 1) = 0$
Since resistance cannot be negative, $R = 2\ \Omega$.

The total resistance of the circuit is the sum of the ladder's equivalent resistance and the battery's internal resistance $r$.
$R_{\text{total}} = R + r = 2 + r$

According to Ohm's law for the complete circuit:
$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{\text{total}}}$
$4 = \dfrac{12}{2 + r}$
$2 + r = 3$
$r = 1\ \Omega$

Answer: $1\ \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, if the positions of the battery and the galvanometer are interchanged, the bridge remains balanced.

Reason (R): The equivalent resistance of the bridge between the battery terminals remains unchanged upon this interchange.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: Let the four arms of the Wheatstone bridge be $P, Q, R,$ and $S$. The condition for a balanced bridge is $\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}$. This equation can be rearranged as $\dfrac{P}{R} = \dfrac{Q}{S}$. When the battery and galvanometer are interchanged, the new adjacent arms become $P, R$ and $Q, S$. Since $\dfrac{P}{R} = \dfrac{Q}{S}$ holds true, the bridge remains balanced. This is known as the reciprocity theorem for a Wheatstone bridge.

Reason (R) is false: The equivalent resistance of the bridge before interchanging the battery and galvanometer is $R_{eq1} = \dfrac{(P+Q)(R+S)}{P+Q+R+S}$. After interchanging, the equivalent resistance becomes $R_{eq2} = \dfrac{(P+R)(Q+S)}{P+Q+R+S}$. In general, $R_{eq1} \neq R_{eq2}$ unless $P=S$ or $Q=R$. Therefore, the equivalent resistance changes.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform metal wire is stretched to double its original length and then bent to form a square. If the equivalent resistance across any two adjacent corners of the square is $15 \Omega$, what was the resistance of the wire before it was stretched?
questions.solution:
Let the original resistance of the unstretched wire be $R_0$.

When the wire is stretched to double its length ($n = 2$), its volume remains constant. The new resistance becomes:
$R_{new} = n^2 R_0 = (2)^2 R_0 = 4 R_0$.

The wire is then bent into a square, which has four equal sides. The resistance of each side of the square is:
$R_{side} = \dfrac{4 R_0}{4} = R_0$.

Across any two adjacent corners, one side is in parallel with the series combination of the remaining three sides.
Resistance of the three sides in series = $R_0 + R_0 + R_0 = 3 R_0$.

The equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ across adjacent corners is:
$R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_0 \times 3 R_0}{R_0 + 3 R_0} = \dfrac{3 R_0^2}{4 R_0} = \dfrac{3}{4} R_0$.

Given that $R_{eq} = 15 \Omega$:
$\dfrac{3}{4} R_0 = 15$
$R_0 = \dfrac{15 \times 4}{3} = 20 \Omega$.

Answer: $20 \Omega$

Resistance of the three sides in series = $R_0 + R_0 + R_0 = 3 R_0$.

The equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ across adjacent corners is:
$R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_0 \times 3 R_0}{R_0 + 3 R_0} = \dfrac{3 R_0^2}{4 R_0} = \dfrac{3}{4} R_0$.

Given that $R_{eq} = 15 \Omega$:
$\dfrac{3}{4} R_0 = 15$
$R_0 = \dfrac{15 \times 4}{3} = 20 \Omega$.

Answer: $20 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A uniform wire AB of resistance $R_0$ is connected across an ideal DC voltage source $V_0$. A resistor $R$ is connected between end A and a sliding contact C on the wire. Let $x$ be the fractional distance of C from A (where $x = \text{AC}/\text{AB}$). Based on this circuit, two statements are given below:

Statement I: As the sliding contact moves from A to B, the potential difference across $R$ increases monotonically.
Statement II: If $R \gg R_0$, the potential difference across $R$ varies approximately linearly with $x$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.solution:
The resistance of segment AC is $x R_0$ and segment CB is $(1-x) R_0$.

The equivalent resistance of AC and $R$ in parallel is $R_p = \dfrac{R (x R_0)}{R + x R_0}$.

The total resistance of the circuit is $R_{eq} = R_p + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R x R_0}{R + x R_0} + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R R_0 + x R_0^2 - x^2 R_0^2}{R + x R_0}$.

The potential difference across $R$ is $V(x) = V_0 \dfrac{R_p}{R_{eq}} = V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R + x(1-x)R_0}$.

To check Statement I, we can write $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{(1-x)R_0}{R}$. As $x$ increases from $0$ to $1$, both $\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $(1-x)$ strictly decrease, so $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)}$ decreases. This means $V(x)$ increases monotonically. Statement I is correct.

For Statement II, if $R \gg R_0$, the term $x(1-x)R_0$ in the denominator can be neglected compared to $R$. Thus, $V(x) \approx V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R} = V_0 x$. This shows a linear relationship with $x$. Statement II is correct.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
questions.question:
A uniform wire AB of resistance $R_0$ is connected across an ideal DC voltage source $V_0$. A resistor $R$ is connected between end A and a sliding contact C on the wire. Let $x$ be the fractional distance of C from A (where $x = \text{AC}/\text{AB}$). Based on this circuit, two statements are given below:

Statement I: As the sliding contact moves from A to B, the potential difference across $R$ increases monotonically.
Statement II: If $R \gg R_0$, the potential difference across $R$ varies approximately linearly with $x$.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
The resistance of segment AC is $x R_0$ and segment CB is $(1-x) R_0$.

The equivalent resistance of AC and $R$ in parallel is $R_p = \dfrac{R (x R_0)}{R + x R_0}$.

The total resistance of the circuit is $R_{eq} = R_p + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R x R_0}{R + x R_0} + (1-x) R_0 = \dfrac{R R_0 + x R_0^2 - x^2 R_0^2}{R + x R_0}$.

The potential difference across $R$ is $V(x) = V_0 \dfrac{R_p}{R_{eq}} = V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R + x(1-x)R_0}$.

To check Statement I, we can write $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x} + \dfrac{(1-x)R_0}{R}$. As $x$ increases from $0$ to $1$, both $\dfrac{1}{x}$ and $(1-x)$ strictly decrease, so $\dfrac{V_0}{V(x)}$ decreases. This means $V(x)$ increases monotonically. Statement I is correct.

For Statement II, if $R \gg R_0$, the term $x(1-x)R_0$ in the denominator can be neglected compared to $R$. Thus, $V(x) \approx V_0 \dfrac{R x}{R} = V_0 x$. This shows a linear relationship with $x$. Statement II is correct.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform wire of resistance $50\ \Omega$ is cut into $5$ equal parts. These parts are then connected in parallel. What is the effective resistance of this parallel combination?
questions.solution:
The resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length ($R \propto l$).

When the wire of resistance $50\ \Omega$ is cut into $5$ equal parts, the resistance of each part becomes:
$R' = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10\ \Omega$

When these $5$ identical parts are connected in parallel, the equivalent resistance $R_{eq}$ is given by:
$R_{eq} = \dfrac{R'}{5} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2\ \Omega$

Answer: $2\ \Omega$

(A) $2\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$(I) $\dfrac{4}{5}$
(B) $3\ \Omega$ and $6\ \Omega$(II) $\dfrac{3}{5}$
(C) $1\ \Omega$ and $4\ \Omega$(III) $\dfrac{1}{2}$
(D) $2\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$(IV) $\dfrac{2}{3}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
When two resistors $R_1$ and $R_2$ are connected in parallel, the current $I_1$ passing through the first resistor $R_1$ is given by the current division rule:
$I_1 = I_{total} \times \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$

For (A) $2\ \Omega$ and $2\ \Omega$: Fraction $= \dfrac{2}{2 + 2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. This matches (III).

For (B) $3\ \Omega$ and $6\ \Omega$: Fraction $= \dfrac{6}{3 + 6} = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. This matches (IV).

For (C) $1\ \Omega$ and $4\ \Omega$: Fraction $= \dfrac{4}{1 + 4} = \dfrac{4}{5}$. This matches (I).

For (D) $2\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$: Fraction $= \dfrac{3}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{3}{5}$. This matches (II).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A) - (III), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (II).

Answer: (A) - (III), (B) - (IV), (C) - (I), (D) - (II)
